subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Upland landscapes in the UK are mostly found in which areas?
questions.explain: Upland landscapes are concentrated in the north and west of the UK, while lowlands dominate the south and east.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a UK upland landscape?
questions.explain: Snowdonia is a mountainous upland area formed of hard, resistant rock in north Wales.

questions.q: Why are upland areas generally found in the north and west of the UK?
options: They are made of older, harder, more resistant rock
They are closer to the equator
They are made mainly of soft clay
questions.explain: Older, harder and more resistant rocks in the north and west erode more slowly, producing higher upland relief.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a UK lowland landscape?
questions.explain: The Fens in East Anglia are a flat, low-lying lowland landscape formed on soft sedimentary deposits.

questions.q: Which process of coastal erosion involves waves throwing sand and pebbles against a cliff face?
questions.explain: Abrasion (corrasion) is when waves hurl sand and pebbles against a cliff, wearing it away.

questions.q: What is the coastal process of attrition?
options: Rock fragments knock together and become smaller and rounder
Sea water dissolves soluble rock such as chalk
Air is compressed in cracks in the cliff by waves
Sediment is carried along the coast by waves
questions.explain: Attrition is when transported rock fragments collide, gradually becoming smaller, smoother and more rounded.

questions.q: Which statement best describes constructive waves?
options: They have a strong swash and weak backwash, building up beaches
They have a strong backwash and weak swash, removing beach material
They are tall, high-frequency waves that erode the coast
They only occur during severe storms
questions.explain: Constructive waves have a powerful swash and weak backwash, so they deposit material and build up beaches.

questions.q: What determines the direction of longshore drift along a coastline?
options: The rock type of the cliffs
questions.explain: The prevailing wind drives waves onto the beach at an angle, so it controls the direction sediment moves by longshore drift.

questions.q: At a place where the coastline suddenly changes direction and sediment is moving along it by longshore drift, which depositional landform is most likely to form?
questions.explain: Where the coastline changes direction, longshore drift deposits sediment out into the sea to form a spit.

questions.q: What is the correct sequence in which erosional landforms develop on a headland?
questions.explain: Erosion widens a crack into a cave, then an arch; the arch collapses to leave a stack, which erodes to a stump.

questions.q: Headlands and bays typically form along which type of coastline?
options: A discordant coastline with alternating bands of hard and soft rock
A concordant coastline made of a single rock type
A coastline made entirely of soft clay
A coastline with no wave action
questions.explain: On a discordant coastline, softer rock erodes faster to form bays while resistant rock is left as headlands.

questions.q: A steep-sided, V-shaped valley in a river's upper course is mainly formed by which process?
questions.explain: In the upper course the river cuts downwards (vertical erosion) while weathering loosens the valley sides to create a V-shape.

questions.q: Which river transport process involves pebbles bouncing along the river bed?
questions.explain: Saltation is the bouncing movement of small stones and pebbles along the river bed.

questions.q: Waterfalls and gorges are landforms typically found in which part of a river's course?
questions.explain: Waterfalls and the gorges left as they retreat form in the upper course where vertical erosion dominates.

questions.q: How does an ox-bow lake form?
options: The narrow neck of a meander is eroded through and later cut off by deposition
A waterfall retreats upstream over time
Levées are breached during a flood
A spit grows across a river mouth
questions.explain: Erosion narrows a meander's neck until the river breaks through, then deposition seals off the old loop as an ox-bow lake.

questions.q: After a river floods and its velocity drops, the coarsest sediment is dropped first along the banks, building up raised ridges. What are these landforms called?
questions.explain: As floodwater slows, the heaviest sediment is deposited nearest the channel, building raised banks called levées.

questions.q: A river is wide, slow-flowing and deposits fine silt across a broad, flat area close to the sea. Which course of the river is this?
questions.explain: A wide, gently sloping channel depositing silt across a floodplain near the sea is characteristic of the lower course.

questions.q: As a river flows from its source to its mouth, what generally happens to the gradient of its long profile?
questions.explain: The long profile is steep near the source and becomes gentler downstream, so the gradient decreases towards the mouth.
